chapter_theme: How to handle enmity as a strategic matter. Don't seek it, avoid certain enemies above all, turn some into friends and others into neutrals, hide your weakness, and cut the rest down while they are still young.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the fault of taking on enmity (871-873), who is to be made friend (874-875), and neutral (876), how to conduct oneself (877), what to do in oneself to remove it (878), when to remove it (879), and the cost of not doing so (880).

871.reading: The thing called enmity, which has no good in it, shouldn't be wanted by anyone, even in jest.
871.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a psychological reason for நகையேயும்: desired in play, the resentment grows and it becomes real. The verse sits at odds with the chapter that comes just before it.

872.reading: Though you take on the enmity of ploughmen whose plough is the bow, do not take on that of ploughmen whose plough is the word.
872.nuance: A famous line, often read now as about writers and poets, but the older commentators don't read it that way. Parimelazhagar means those with counsel and policy, whose harm reaches one's descendants, and Manakkudavar means ministers. Kalaignar's 'learned' is the broadest. Both groups are 'ploughmen', borrowing the honour chapter 104 gives to that work.

873.reading: One who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many is more wretched than those who are ஏமுற்றவர்.

positions.position: ஏமுற்றவர் are the mad, who at least aren't harmed by their delusion, while this one is.
positions.quote: மயக்கத்தால் ஒப்பாராயினும் ஏமுற்றவர் அதனால் தீங்கு எய்தாமையின்

positions.position: ஏமுற்றவர் are the arrogant, and this person is better called a fool than arrogant.
positions.quote: ஆணவம் பிடித்தவன் என்பதைவிட அறிவிலி என்பதே பொருத்தமாகும்.

874.reading: The world rests in the greatness of a person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship.
874.nuance: நட்பாக் கொண்டு is ambiguous: making them friends, or treating them as friends? The whole verse turns on it.

positions.position: A king who, when it is needed, wins enemies over, and whose power therefore holds the world.
positions.quote: வேண்டியவழிப் பகையை வேறுபடுத்துத் தனக்கு நட்பாகச் செய்து கொண்டொழுகும் இயல்பினையுடைய அரசனது

positions.position: One able to behave toward enemies as if they were friends.
It is a moral nobility in anyone who thinks of enemies as friends, and the world praises it.
positions.quote: பகைவர்களையும் நண்பர்களாகக் கருதிப் பழகுகின்ற பெருந்தன்மையான பண்பை

875.reading: If you have no ally and two enemies, being alone, take one of them as a pleasing ally.
875.nuance: The word is இன்துணை, a sweet ally, which is warm for what it describes. Parimelazhagar adds 'for that time', and picks the one suited to defeating the other. The temporariness is his addition, though it's probably correct as politics.

876.reading: Whether or not you have trusted him, when ruin comes neither join with him nor break from him; let him be.
876.nuance: A rule for neutrality. Parimelazhagar explains the two halves separately: don't join, because he could harm from inside; don't break, because he could help your ruin along. In adversity an enemy is best left unprovoked.

877.reading: Don't complain to those who don't know of your pain, and don't show softness in front of enemies.
877.nuance: The pairing is the surprise. Parimelazhagar takes those who don't know to be friends who haven't noticed on their own, which is itself a judgement on them. Pain should be read and not announced, which ties this to the chapters on signs.

878.reading: Knowing the way, building oneself up and guarding oneself will end the swagger on the enemy's side.
878.nuance: All three verbs are about oneself and none about the enemy, yet the enemy is what changes. Parimelazhagar's enemy is celebrating an expected win. Manakkudavar calls this 'the way to kill enemies', which shows how much he thinks self-strengthening does.

879.reading: Cut a thorn tree while it is young; grown hard, it will destroy the hand that cuts it.
879.nuance: The verse itself doesn't mention enemies, and Parimelazhagar labels it allegory. Its logic of acting before a threat matures has no room in it for what a sapling might have become, or for whether it is really a thorn.

880.reading: Those who don't break the pride of those hostile to them are, surely, not alive even to breathe.
880.nuance: Parimelazhagar adds that this is about one who could do it and neglects it out of contempt.

positions.position: Their enemies will grow and destroy them, so they won't live even long enough to draw breath. He allows that it may be the enemy's breath that kills.
positions.quote: அவர் உயிர்த்த துணையானே தாம் இறப்பர் எனினும் அமையும்.

positions.position: It is the enemy's breath that kills, and the lesson is not to take on the strong as enemies at all.
positions.quote: இது பகை கொள்ளுங்கால் வலியாரோடு பகைகோடலாகா தென்றது.

positions.position: They can't be said to live merely because they are breathing.
positions.quote: சுவாசிக்கிற காரணத்தினாலேயே, உயிரோடிருப்பதாக நிச்சயமாகச் சொல்ல முடியாது.

links.note: 874 says the world rests on the one who turns enemies into friends. 830 says that when an enemy turns friend, give only your face and drop even that later. If this is the same event seen from both sides, then each party in 874's triumph has reason to be following 830.

852 and its chapter say it is best not to return harm and to lean away from hostility. 879 says to kill the threat while it is young. One counsels letting enmity die by itself and the other warns that it won't, and both claim the outcome is self-preservation.

In 763 the rats die when the cobra merely breathes (உயிர்ப்ப). In 880 those who don't break a foe's pride don't survive his breath (on Manakkudavar's reading). The word for breathing is the unit of how little it takes.

Both warn against telling pain to those not attuned to it. In 877 it is a matter of strategy and self-respect, and in 1200 the lover scolds her own heart for telling sorrow to one who doesn't care. The advice carries across books, and it is much sadder in the second one.
